1. Most Important Skill: Clear communication and precise thinking - explain exactly to the AI what you want and what’s important.
2. Create a Good Environment: Clean codebases and tests are crucial (“garbage in, garbage out”); specifications that focus solely on theory without considering code often fail.
3. Uncover Unknown Gaps: Be aware of “unknown unknowns - by having the AI interview you before it builds anything.
4. Trust Ladder: Don’t trust blindl - start small, monitor closely, and only gradually grant more autonomy.
5. Delegate routine tasks: Use AI primarily for boring, repetitive tasks so you can focus on what matters most.

Matt is spot on when he say that provisioning information (context) to coding agents in a systematic and reproducible manner is critically important (and extremely hard to get right). I've spent so much time designing different systems to do this, but they all seem to fail some way or another. 1) Must be easy to add data. Matt uses an inbox for docs to digest. That is super convenient, but goes against seperation of concerns. You need complete trust in the system, to not place docs inside the projects they concern. 2) The file digestion is inherently a lossy process and some docs cannot be safely reduced as they could hold agent outputs that are 'key findings' or other destillations that should go in exactly as they are. 3). Finding the right balance between a minimal index/wiki (to avoid bloating the context window) and yet provide enough information in the wiki for an agent know where to go for deeper dives when needed. 4) Find out when and how an agent goes to the raw file for ultimate information when needed. In practice the digest becomes the ground truth which is risky. 5) How to avoid the coding agent anchoring heavily on random shit you dumped in the brain at some point. It must be very easy for the agent to assess the quality of a doc. This makes it risky to dump loose ideas and abandoned projects as your coding agent will often think that those constitute something to model after. And metadata is not even truly enforcable with an LLM, so you never know when it just ignores metadata warnings. Just mentioning other projects in the wiki will see your agent rummage around old crappy projects trying to find some random stuff to model after. I constantly had to turn off the wiki when needing the model to think unanchored (which I very often do).

My latest approach (to be implemented) is using nested brains. Small local brains are much easier to get right for a single project. No need to have 'names', 'colleagues', 'topics' and stuff like that in a single app repo. These small brains can become linked to parent brains which work the same but at a higher level. Wish me luck 🙂

I kind of caught wind of the idea of optimizing your environment that the agent works in a couple weeks ago. There's this other guy on YouTube (I can't remember his name) but I believe he's somewhat involved in academia or AI research and machine learning research. He was really big on, similar to what Matt talks about, the environment (basically the folder system) that you have your agent work in is paramount.

It's kind of been an idea that's been bouncing around in my head with the different harnesses like Codex and Claude Code. It kind of comes down to this: having the ability for skills in those harnesses is good but you could just basically do the same thing without skills in those harnesses. You could essentially just have read-me files or text documents linked if you have your folder structure set up the right way.

It really is kind of seeing that everything's shifting towards environment for agents and that's how you get a different type of agent rather than creating these custom agents. You could just use one model, open it up in a folder system, and if you have that folder system set up in a manner that agents know what you like and what's important to you (like Matt says), everything kind of goes a lot more smoothly and you don't really need that much effort.

Also since the Claude 5 models, I've been trimming down a lot of my context that agents have access to. It seems to be working pretty well. This was an interesting conversation between you two. I enjoyed it. Really got some gears going in my head.
